title: late-binding-kernel-routing-scratchpad
content:
Goal: quick, messy brain dump on the idea of late-binding kernel routing for mixed-precision / mixed-kernel serving. This is a personal scratchpad — rough experiments to try, intuition, and questions to bring to the applied-ml sync.

Background / motivating observation:
- In production we serve a variety of request shapes: short chat turns (<=128 tokens), medium prompts (512-1024), and long-context completions (>2048).
- Different kernel implementations (flash-attention variants, int8 quantized matmuls, fused-kv-cache copies) have different sweet spots. A single statically-chosen kernel for all requests is suboptimal.
- Idea: defer final kernel selection until just before execution ("late-binding") and choose per-request (or per-batch) the kernel path that maximizes throughput within latency SLO and memory constraints.

Reading notes (papers / posts I skimmed in the past couple weeks):
- FlashAttention variants: benefits when sequence length and batch size are high; but memory access pattern matters for KV cache copying.
- Quantization papers: per-channel vs per-tensor int8 tradeoffs; some 4-bit recipes keep activations in fp16 for attention and only quantize matmuls.
- Kernel switching: limited literature — most infra projects pick kernels at compile-time or model-load time. There are some short workshop notes on adaptive kernel dispatching that argue for runtime micro-benchmarks.

Hypothesis sketch:
- Maintain a tiny on-host profiler that benchmarks candidate kernels for a small set of representative shapes (sequence lengths: 32, 128, 512, 2048; batch sizes: 1, 4, 16).
- For each incoming request, map it to a representative shape bucket and pick the kernel with best predicted tokens/sec given current GPU occupancy and cache state.
- When batches contain mixed shapes, try two strategies: 1) pad to max shape in batch and pick kernel optimized for that padded shape; 2) dynamic-sharding: group by shape within the batch and run sub-batches sequentially with different kernels (might increase overall latency but improve throughput).

Concrete experiments to run (low-cost first):
1) Microbench runner: implement microbench harness to run candidate kernels on a single GPU for the shapes above and collect latency, memory, and occupancy metrics. Try to re-use the runtime's existing triton/cuda wrapper. (Owner: me).
2) Simulated dispatcher: create a small simulation that given microbench results and a synthetic traffic trace (sampled from our logs) predicts average tokens/sec and 95th p99 latency under different routing policies. (Owner: Iris).
3) Live A/B: integrate dispatcher into an internal staging instance and route a small % of traffic. Compare cost (GPU-hours / token) and p99 latency vs baseline. (Owner: Maya).

Metric definitions and success criteria:
- Primary: p50/p95/p99 latency per token and tokens/sec (throughput).
- Secondary: GPU utilization, memory oversubscription events, number of kernel switches per-second (overhead).
- Success: reduce cost-per-token by 8–15% while keeping p95 <= current SLO or trading off only at tails with graceful degradation.

Runtime engineering notes / constraints:
- Kernel warm-start cost: cold kernel launches (first-time invocation) can add tens of ms — need to pre-warm or account for it in decisions.
- Memory fragmentation: switching between kernels that use different workspace sizes can cause fragmentation and OOM unless we adopt a pooling strategy.
- Compatibility matrix: not all kernels are valid for quantized weights or fused rotary embeddings; need to maintain a capability matrix per model variant.
- Telemetry: record kernel_id, shape_bucket, chosen_policy, and latency for each request (for offline analysis). Keep this lightweight.

Potential failure modes / open questions:
- Oscillation: dispatcher might flip-flop between kernels on short timescales if metrics are noisy. Need smoothing and hysteresis.
- Mixed-precision correctness drift: switching to lower-precision kernels occasionally causes output divergence — need a lightweight quality check (hash of logits or small eval set) to detect regressions.
- Multi-tenant GPUs: current scheduling in Dedicated makes occupancy unpredictable; dispatcher needs to incorporate instantaneous reserved occupancy signals if available.

Quick sketch of design doc sections to draft next:
- Motivation and traffic characterization (include histograms from logs)
- Kernel capability matrix and how to populate it automatically
- Offline microbench harness and how to parametrize it per hardware family
- Runtime dispatcher: policy API, smoothing, and telemetry
- Rollout plan: start in-staging -> small % in prod -> safety fallback to baseline kernel

Notes-to-self / small hacks to try now:
- Reuse the existing per-model quantization profile code to tag which kernels are allowed for a model.
- Add a tiny shim in the runtime that can intercept kernel selection; start by exposing an env var to force selection to test switching overhead.
- Add a synthetic trace generator that mirrors the worst 5% traffic (long-context bursts) — stress test memory fragmentation.

Links / quick refs:
- internal PR: github.com/redwood-inference/inference-runtime/pull/482 (perf harness)
- internal confluence stub: CONFLUENCE-RT/KB-routing-design
- metrics query to pull representative shapes: JIRA-RT-1273 has the sql snippet we used in Aug 2027

Questions for 1:1 with Iris (agenda):
- How stable are microbench numbers across contention? Do we need to rebench every 6 hours?
- What is the cheapest way to record per-request kernel telemetry without increasing our logs by 10x?

Bottom line (for now): promising small win if we can cheaply and reliably pick kernels per-shape without adding oscillation or fragmentation. Next step: get the microbench harness merged and run it overnight on a p4dish cluster to gather baseline numbers.

- [ ] Build simulation using sample traffic (Iris)
- [ ] Draft helm flag and runtime shim (Maya)

-- Oliver
